Gavin Baker on the other side of Ben's bandwidth story: at the peak of the 2000 bubble, 97% of America's fiber sat dark, and today there are no dark GPUs.

"I had, depending on how you look at it, the privilege and the misfortune of being a tech investor during the year 2000 bubble, which was really a telecom bubble."

"The year 2000 bubble was defined by something called 'dark fiber.' Dark fiber was literally fiber that was laid down in the ground, and not lit up... At the peak of the bubble, 97% of the fiber that had been laid in America was dark."

"Contrast that with today. There are no dark GPUs. All you have to do is read any technical paper, and one of the biggest problems in a training run is that GPUs are melting."

@GavinSBaker

Non-asset owners are seeing a large drop in US consumer sentiment.

Since January 2026, consumer sentiment is down -27% among the bottom 33% of stockholders, the largest decline among the stock-wealth groups surveyed.

This is followed by those who do not own stocks, whose sentiment is down -25% over the same period.

By comparison, sentiment is down just -9% among the middle 33% and -7% among the top 33% of stockholders.

Asset ownership has helped offset the impact of higher living costs, leaving consumers with fewer or no stocks more exposed to the recent acceleration in inflation.

Meanwhile, 1-year consumer inflation expectations rose +0.1 percentage point this month, to 4.7%, its 2nd-highest reading since August 2025.

Own assets or be left behind.

Ali Ghodsi of @Databricks on the four conditions that would have to hold for AI to truly improve itself:

"The next model requires less resources, less GPUs to train... The second condition: the next model takes less time to train as well. Third, accuracy of the model, the intelligence is increasing. And fourth, we can do the former three again and again and again... All at the same time, not just any of them."

"If you just mean that the software is writing itself, we're already there today. Like 90-some percent of the software in Databricks is written by AI. Does it matter if the last few percent is also written by AI? No."

"If you're getting these four conditions, then you might get a speed-up where the next model, let's say, takes half amount of time and half the resources, and it is more intelligent... By the way, I don't even know if that necessarily leads you to superintelligence."

"A lot of people, their definition is just, 'Hey, if I'm not even coding anymore and it's coding itself'... I think they're conflating, 'Hey, what's my value and is it scary for me?' Versus, 'Hey, that then means we'll get that superintelligence that in 2014 was hypothesized by Bostrom.'"

@alighodsi @martin_casado @sarah_wang

tweets.text:
Ben Horowitz on the lesson LoudCloud, his early cloud company, taught him about today's AI neoclouds, and why they now face the opposite problem:

"It can end up being like a very dangerous arbitrage business, where you can get upside-down easily. And so if you look at LoudCloud, just as an example, here's a simple thing that happened to us."

"In 1999, bandwidth was $1,500 a megabit. And you couldn't get it. It was very hard to get it. And so you had to get a long-term contract, three years. By 2001, it was $50 a megabit... And if you borrowed money to get it, you're dead."

"That kind of thing is so out of the control of the entrepreneur."

"I think the core dynamic of AI has been working for CoreWeave, though, in that there's a massive shortage, not an overage of supply... Token prices have gone down, but GPU prices have not."

"And by the way, data center space is going up in price because even labor to build data centers is hard. The politics are making it hard to build data centers. So the whole supply chain price is going up and demand is not subsiding."

"Those are very big tailwinds for CoreWeave, despite the fact that the debt markets, kind of independent of them, are tough."

@bhorowitz w/ @chamath on @allinpod

BREAKING: Interest expense on US public debt rose +$144 billion YoY in FY2026, or +12%, to a record $1.36 trillion.

This marks the 6th consecutive annual increase, for a total of +$839 billion, or +161%.

For perspective, total receipts rose just +3.2% YoY, to $5.40 trillion.

In other words, interest on federal debt accounted for 25% of total US government receipts.

Meanwhile, Social Security, the largest government expense, jumped +$86 billion YoY, or +5.5%, to a record $1.67 trillion.

At this pace, interest costs will exceed Social Security as the largest government outlay by the end of 2028.

What is the long-term plan here?

tweets.text: Good Morning from Germany, where the Left, Greens & SPD have successfully concluded exploratory talks and will move to coalition negotiations in Berlin, pending party approval. Their housing deal: expropriate large landlords’ holdings above 10,000 homes, exempt homes built since 2021, and cap total compensation at €16bn. If that ceiling cannot be met, no expropriation. They also pledge 100,000 new homes. The stakes for Vonovia: ~138,000 Berlin apartments valued at €27.5bn, or 27% of its property portfolio. These are assets exposed, not projected losses. But compensation below market value could destroy shareholder value and tighter rent regulation could squeeze cash flows even if expropriation never happens.

French government debt exceeds 100% of GDP and continues to rise. 

The country has one of the lowest retirement ages in the world and one of the most generous pension systems.

If France had a fast growing economy, it could provide for its aging population. But it does not. Real GDP was flat in Q2 after shrinking by 0.2% in Q1. Growth has averaged only 1.1% since the start of 2023. 

France’s productivity performance has been abysmal. Real output per hour worked has grown by a total of only 1.5% since 2015, compared with 20.3% in the US.

Like other European countries, France faces a challenging demographic outlook. The total fertility rate fell to 1.56 in 2025, the lowest level since the end of World War I.

The immigration system is failing. Employment rates among immigrants are considerably lower than those of the rest of the population. According to the OECD, nearly half of second-generation students (those born in France) are innumerate.

This week’s Chief Economist’s View report discusses the outlook for France,
as well as where we are in the AI capex cycle, recent trends in inflation and bond yields, and much more. 

Clients can access the report here:

https://t.co/0E36uC2bLE
